text: The bags are overweight.
There's a small fee. She pays it.
Dawn Michelle Hunt, from Chicago, on a trip she thinks she's won.
Waiting to board, she's called aside.
Her brother told lawmakers what she told him.
Methamphetamine, authorities say.
Her family says she had no idea.
She thought the handbags were a prize.
The bags were checked in her name.
The drugs, she said, were not hers.
Three years later, a court sentences her to death, with a two-year reprieve.
Today, she is serving life.
Twelve years on, he told a congressional commission this.
His written statement says she keeps asking him the same question.
Before China, there was Chicago.
Dawn was a daughter and a sister. A former flight attendant. An artist who loved fashion, and travel.
Her brother describes her as intelligent, and trusting. She loved entering sweepstakes with their mother, he told Reuters.
She came from a family of Chicago police officers. Her father, Gene, served thirty-two years. Tim served twenty-eight. Their mother and three uncles had been officers too, the commission was told.
Then an email told her she'd won.
His written statement calls the prize cash.
She told her father, too.
She sent them her passport details, Tim wrote. They sent her a ticket.
The first part of the promise was true.
The email became a ticket. The ticket became a city. And the city became trust.
Each time, she said yes. And each yes took her a step closer to that room.
Her luggage was already full, Tim wrote. So she went with some of the people who organized her trip to the Baiyun Leather Market, and the organizers bought her an extra bag.
Two pieces of luggage. She checked both.
At the check-in desk, the scale said what you already know.
Overweight. She paid the fee.
"...she even paid a small excess weight fee," he wrote.
The fee. The yes. The bags she packed. Every one of those details, we have from her brother.
Whatever was sewn into those linings was now checked in her name.
In the room, the officers ask whether the bags are hers.
They ask again.
She checked them herself. To her, they're her bags.
Then they find what's inside the linings.
Two conversations, in one room. In her account, she is identifying her luggage. The officers are investigating drug smuggling.
The same room. The same bags. The same word. Two different meanings.
More than two kilograms of methamphetamine, about four and a half pounds, authorities say.
One detail is unresolved.
Dawn told him she was flying to Australia. A journalist, he wrote, said a court record has her on an internal flight, to Qingdao.
He doesn't know why. Neither do we.
What her brother and the authorities both say: drugs were found in luggage she had checked. She was arrested and charged with smuggling, a charge her brother says she vehemently denies.
The trip ended in that room. The case was only beginning.
She would spend about three years in detention before any verdict.
She cooperated, he wrote. She answered all their questions, and handed over the emails the organizers had sent her.

In 2024, Tim told the commission that Dawn had told their father she was sexually assaulted in the detention facility. When he asked her about it on a prison visit, with someone beside her listening, she said no. He said he knew she was under duress. The allegation has not been independently established.
The State Department's advice today: do not transport unfamiliar gifts, luggage or packages across borders.
She trusted the organizers. For more than two weeks, they had put together her trip.
The words matter. It was a suspended death sentence, not an order for her immediate execution. It was later reduced to life in prison.

China sees a serious crime. In 2026, its foreign ministry told Reuters that she and another American are serving sentences for serious drug-related crimes, handled according to the rule of law, with their health and legitimate rights protected.
Her family insists she was what investigators call a blind mule: someone who carries drugs for traffickers without knowing it.
According to her family, and to reporting on the court's reasoning, the judge recognised that she had been deceived, and concluded that she should have known anyway.
Deceived.
And guilty anyway.
In June 2024, her brother was let in to see her.
Guangdong Women's Prison. It had taken him six to eight months to get permission.
He found a sister who had lost weight, and was very pale.

Doctors who examined her in prison, he said, had found uterine fibroids, and possibly ovarian cancer: not a confirmed diagnosis. She had needed numerous transfusions for heavy bleeding, and had been advised to have a hysterectomy. She refused, out of distrust.
She still had to work, he said, making lithium batteries.
Later, a senator asked him about that visit. Armed guards with long guns had escorted him, he said. They held his passport during the visit.
Gene Hunt was, in his son's words, an American of Americans. He had served in the Army, worked as a skimmer in the steel mills, and driven a Chicago bus, before thirty-two years in the police.
As a boy, Tim wrote, he watched his father save the next-door neighbours from a house fire.
There was one person Gene could not bring home.

In May 2025, Tim says, the United States asked for her release on humanitarian grounds. That September, a bipartisan bill was introduced in Congress, named for her and for Nelson Wells Junior, another American held in China.
None of it brought her home.
On January 25th, 2026, Gene Hunt died. He was ninety-two.
He never saw Dawn come home.
That July, though he had told the commission it wouldn't be advisable, Tim went back.
In September, he sat before the commission again.
Some things had improved, he told them. More visits. A few books.
He described a sister who had aged dramatically: slumped over, frail, her teeth yellowed and shifted, her hair much greyer.
Two years earlier, he had spared his father some of the details. Now there was no father to spare.
But there was one thing she kept coming back to.
She wants a date.
When he tells her that, he wrote, she becomes angry. All of this, she says, has only filled her head with false hopes.
Twelve years ago, officers asked Dawn a question. She answered it.
Now she's the one asking. And no one has given her a date.
As of November 2026, Dawn Michelle Hunt is still in prison in China. Her family, and the State Department, are still calling for her release on humanitarian grounds.
